title: Ang 1278–1284: Malar ki Var
hookLine: Guru Nanak's ballad in Malar, first half
tomorrow: what does the rain ballad tell you to throw in the fire?

lines: RAIN ON THE JUST AND THE UNJUST.
cards: Maya's family has Simran over for a goodbye dinner, and halfway through the lasagna the sky opens again.
Maya's grandmother, who keeps verses taped to her fridge, watches the window for a moment and says one from memory: he sends rain on the just and on the unjust. Then she passes the bread.
Simran drives home with the wipers going, turning it over. So is rain good news, or isn't it? Guru Nanak answers in a ballad.

teach.b: Malar ki Var, Guru Nanak's ballad in the raga of the rains, begins on ang 1278. A page in, two short saloks look at one storm from two sides.
In paraphrase: if it rains in Saavan, the rainy month, four are glad: the snakes, the deer, the fish, and the well-off, snug at home.
If it rains in Saavan, four feel the separation: the calves, the poor, the traveler on the road, and the servant.
Same rain. Different lives. The salok's answer is that the storm isn't one thing, and it asks you to see both lists.
Now the verse at Maya's grandmother's table.

teach.h: MATTHEW: RAIN ON THE JUST AND UNJUST.
teach.b: It's from the Sermon on the Mount, in the Gospel of Matthew, where Jesus says God “maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.”
Here's what they share: both look at the same sky and see that the rain falls on everyone, earned by no one.

In Matthew, the rain is God's generosity to all, given as the reason to love even your enemies. In the salok, the rain is the same for all, but it lands differently, and the eye goes to the ones standing out in it.

One asks you to give the way the rain gives. The other asks you to notice who's getting wet. Something to tell a friend tonight: a grandmother's fridge and a Guru's ballad, looking at the same weather.

how: Sikhs sing the pauris and saloks of Malar ki Var in kirtan; the rain saloks on ang 1279 are found in Guru Nanak's ballad under the heading Malar ki Var Mahala 1.

games.q: one storm, two sides — tap the pairs.
p: the rainy month the salok names
rain on the just and on the unjust

s: in Malar ki Var, Guru Nanak says rain is good news for everyone
four are glad, four feel the separation: same rain, different lives.
the verse on Maya's grandmother's fridge comes from the Sermon on the Mount
Matthew: God sends rain on the just and on the unjust.
the salok and the verse in Matthew make exactly the same point
both see rain fall on all; Matthew draws love for enemies, the salok notices who's out in it.

games.q: pouring rain on the way to school. you're dry in a car; a kid you know is waiting at an open bus stop. with the rain ballad in mind, what comes first?
o: notice who's out in the rain, then do what you can.
be thankful; rain is good news if you're comfortable.
it rains on everyone alike, so it all evens out.
games.why: Guru Nanak's saloks set the same rain against two lists: the glad and the separated. the ballad asks you to see both, and the ones standing out in it.

practice: Count, on the fingers of one hand, four things that make today easy for you. Then count, on the other hand, four people for whom today is hard: someone on the road, someone working outside, someone far from home, someone you know.
Rest with both hands open on your lap, one list in each.
